## Introduction

Every morning, millions of people reach for a moisturizer, a foundation, a mascara, a lip gloss, and other cosmetics before 8am. We trust these products completely. They smell good, they feel good, and they come in beautiful packaging. But buried inside many of those sleek bottles and colorful palettes are ingredients that scientists and public health researchers have flagged as potentially harmful.

Cosmetics in the U.S. do not need FDA approval before they are sold. Companies decide what is safe and most of us have no idea what is actually in our products.

## Data

The data comes from the California Safe Cosmetics Program (CSCP), run by the California Department of Public Health. It requires cosmetic companies selling in California to report any products containing chemicals linked to cancer, birth defects, or reproductive harm. The dataset covers 2009 to 2020 and includes over 114,000 records across 36,972 unique products.

I wanted to turn this data into something anyone could read and learn from. So, I built an infographic around following four questions:

**Which harmful chemicals show up most often across cosmetic products?**

**Which companies have the largest number of reported products?**

**Which luxury brands expose consumers to the widest variety of harmful chemicals?**

**Which popular brands has less harmful chemicals?**

You can [explore the full dataset here](https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/chemicals-in-cosmetics-d55bf).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Infographic

![The chemistry of beauty: An infographic exploring harmful chemicals in cosmetic products reported to the California Safe Cosmetics Program between 2009 and 2020.](infographic.png)

My final infographic has four visualizations, all built in R using `{ggplot2}` and assembled in Affinity Designer.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Design Process

### 1. Graphic Form

I used four chart types, each chosen for a specific reason.

The **warning icon list** for the top 5 chemicals keeps the ranking simple and readable. Each entry has the chemical name and the exact product count so the scale is immediately clear.

The **makeup brush bar chart** for the top 10 companies uses horizontal bars with a makeup brush image overlaid in Affinity Designer. Company names are long and hard to read on a vertical axis, so i did `coord_flip()`. The brush image gives the chart cosmetics theme.

The **luxury brand bubble chart** is styled to look like a blush palette. Each bubble is one brand, sized by number of products reported. The palette aesthetic felt natural for a chart about luxury beauty brands.

The **popular brands treemap** is styled to look like an eyeshadow palette. Each box is one brand, sized by number of products. The treemap makes it easy to compare brands at a glance without needing to read every number.

### 2. Text (Titles, Labels, Annotations)

Every chart has a direct title that states what it shows. Labels are placed directly on the chart so readers do not have to look back and forth between the data and a legend.

The woman thinking "Which one to buy?" ties the whole infographic together. After seeing all the data, that is the natural question on readers mind. The annotation next to her, "Affordable favorites with 300+ products shows an unexpected pattern in chemical use," gives the reader one last thing to think about.

### 3. Themes

All charts use a clean white background with no gridlines. I kept the layout minimal so the cosmetics-themed design elements carry the visual weight without competing with the data.

### 4. Colors

I built a custom palette called **Velvet Dawn**: muted roses, warm sands, dusty wines, slate indigo, dusty brick red, and pale ivory. The palette is inspired by the cosmetics world, soft and warm rather than clinical.

``` r
palette <- c(
  "rose"   = "#D8A7B1",  # Rose Dust
  "sand"   = "#E6C9A8",  # Warm Sand
  "plum"   = "#8E6A7A",  # Muted Plum
  "almond" = "#F5E6D8",  # Pale Almond
  "wine"   = "#9B4A5A",  # Dusty Wine
  "sky"    = "#A8BED1",  # Hazy Sky
  "olive"  = "#9DA87A",  # Muted Olive
  "butter" = "#EDD9A3",  # Pale Butter
  "indigo" = "#7B7DB5",  # Slate Indigo
  "brick"  = "#B85C5C"   # Dusty Brick Red
)
```

The colors are not perfectly colorblind friendly in every combination, but every key finding is also encoded through labels, position, and text so color is never the only way to read the chart.

### 5. Typography

I used two fonts:

-   **Jost** for all data labels, counts, and annotations inside R
-   **Noteworthy** for display and decorative text inside Affinity Designer

Fonts were loaded in R using `font_add_google()` from `{sysfonts}` and activated with `showtext_auto()`.

### 6. General Design

The four panels are ordered deliberately. You start with what chemicals are in products, move to which companies are responsible, then compare luxury brands, and end with popular brands. Each panel raises the next question naturally.

The woman thinking "Which one to buy?" at the bottom is the closing moment. After seeing all the data, the reader is left with the same question every consumer has.

Both brand charts are filtered to brands with at least 30 products to avoid small brands skewing the results.

### 7. Contextualizing the Data

The infographic opens with a plain statement of the problem: cosmetics in the U.S. do not need FDA approval before they are sold. That framing is there so readers understand why this data matters before they look at any chart.

The definition of harmful chemicals is stated directly inside the infographic: ingredients linked to cancer, birth defects, or reproductive harm, required by California law to be reported.

### 8. Centering the Primary Message

The central message is that harmful chemicals are widespread in cosmetics across all price points. The most famous luxury brands are not always clean, even though they are very expensive. And affordable favorites show unexpected patterns too.

### 9. Accessibility

Font sizes are large enough to read without zooming. Every key finding is backed up by explicit labels and counts, not just visual size or color. Alt text is provided for the infographic image.

### 10. DEI Lens

The data covers products reported to the CSCP between 2009 and 2020. It reflects what companies chose to report, not a complete picture of every harmful ingredient in every product on the market. Some companies may have underreported.

The infographic focuses on consumer exposure because the people most affected by this data are everyday shoppers, not regulators.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Reflections

The finding that surprised me most was in the luxury brand chart. Dior leads with 6 chemical types and 367 reported products, more than Chanel, Givenchy, or Estee Lauder. Price is clearly not a reliable signal of how clean a product is.

The hardest part of this project was cleaning the brand names. The raw dataset has 2,573 unique brand name entries for what is actually a much smaller set of real brands. "Parfums Chrisitian Dior", "Parfums Christain Dior", and "Parfums Christian Dior" are three separate entries for the same brand, all with different typos. Collapsing those variants using `str_detect()` inside `case_when()` took more time than building any single chart.

The cosmetics-themed design came together in Affinity Designer after all the charts were built in R. Laying the makeup brush over the bar chart and styling the bubble and treemap charts as eyeshadow palettes gave the infographic a visual identity that felt right for the topic.

## Explore the Code

All visualizations were built in R using `{ggplot2}`, `{packcircles}`, `{ggtext}`, `{showtext}`, and `{glue}`. The full code is available in the expandable chunk below.

```{r}
#| label: load-packages
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(janitor)
library(scales)
library(lubridate)
library(tidyverse)
library(showtext)
library(sysfonts)
library(glue)
library(packcircles)
library(ggtext)
library(treemapify)
library(here)
```

```{r}
#| label: import-fonts
#| echo: true

font_add_google(name = "Jost", family = "jost")
font_add(family  = "fa-brands",
         regular = here::here("fonts", "Font Awesome 7 Brands-Regular-400.otf"))
font_add(family  = "fa-solid",
         regular = here::here("fonts", "Font Awesome 7 Free-Solid-900.otf"))

showtext_auto()
showtext_opts(dpi = 300)
```

```{r}
#| label: read-data
#| echo: true
#| output: false

cscp_data <- read_csv(here::here("data", "cscpopendata.csv")) %>%
  clean_names()
```

```{r}
#| label: data-cleaning
#| echo: true

cscp_clean <- cscp_data %>%
  mutate(
    initial_date_reported     = mdy(initial_date_reported),
    most_recent_date_reported = mdy(most_recent_date_reported),
    discontinued_date         = mdy(discontinued_date),
    chemical_created_at       = mdy(chemical_created_at),
    chemical_updated_at       = mdy(chemical_updated_at),
    chemical_date_removed     = mdy(chemical_date_removed)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    report_year  = year(initial_date_reported),
    report_month = month(initial_date_reported, label = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(
    c(primary_category, sub_category, chemical_name, company_name, brand_name),
    str_trim
  )) %>%
  filter(!is.na(chemical_name))
```
